items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to requiring child day care facilities to post a copy of the most recent inspection report
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5676

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the social services law, in relation
to requiring child day care facilities to post a copy of the most
recent inspection report

Purpose:

To bring accountability standards for New York City daycare centers
into line with those for daycares throughout the rest of New York by
requiring them to post information regarding their latest health and
safety inspection in a prominent place, thereby providing vital
information to parents choosing daycare facilities for their children.

Summary of Provisions:

Section 1: Amends Social Services Law section 390-i to apply to those
child day care programs licensed or registered pursuant to article 47
of the New York City health code by the Department of Health and
Mental Hygiene of the city of New York.

Section 2: Effective date: the first of January following the day on
which it shall have become law; provided that any rules and
regulations necessary to implement the law have been authorized on or
before such date.

Justification:

Daycare centers in New York State are regulated and licensed by the
Office of Children and Family Services, but those that operate within
New York City fall under the jurisdiction of the City Department of
Health and Mental Hygiene. While those under state jurisdiction are
held accountable for their performance during annual health and safety
inspections, those administered by the City are not, and parents there
may be unknowingly leaving their young children in the care of
irresponsible and dangerous daycares that continue to operate despite
being consistently cited for violations.

According to data provided by the Department of Health and Mental
Hygiene, group day care centers in New York were cited for over 15,000
violations between 2013 and 2014 - with the worst offenders racking up
more than 50 violations apiece in that time span.  Furthermore, many
of these violations create dangerous environments where the safety of
children is at risk: such as neglecting to conduct mandated background
checks on employees, failure to provide constant qualified
supervision, or failure to inspect and maintain fire extinguishers.

Unfortunately, many of these violations are not only severe, but also
recurring. According to inspection reports maintained by the
Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, 237 daycares throughout New
York City remain in operation despite being cited for violations in
100% of their annual inspections, and 88 of them have been cited for
identical violations during numerous inspections - demonstrating that
they are not committed to providing safe and effective care.

Thousands of parents throughout New York City are potentially
unknowingly placing the safety and education of their young children


in the hands of unqualified, dangerous daycare centers that refuse to
learn their lesson and continue to provide unsafe or unsuitable
accommodations to young children despite receiving multiple warnings
from authorities. By requiring New York City daycare centers to adhere
to the same standards that the rest of the state's childcare providers
must meet - posting information about their recent inspection results
so parents can see it - we can help inform parents which day care
centers truly have the best interests of their children at heart.

Legislative History:

New Bill

Fiscal Implications:

None

Effective Date:

January 1 following the date the bill is made law.

A.actClause: AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to the establishment of a performance summary card for child care services in a city having a population of one million or more
A.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S5676A

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the social services law, in relation to the
establishment of a performance summary card for child care services in
a city having a population of one million or more

 PURPOSE :

This bill requires that permitted child care services inside the City
of New York must post a performance summary card which contains
information regarding the results of their previous inspections from
the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH).

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1: Defines the performance summary card and states that it
shall summarize recent inspection violations and programs suspensions
as required by rules issued by DOHMH. Also states that the cards may
include additional information, such as the capacity of the child care
service, the length of time the service operated, a comparison of the
child care service to other child care services in the same social
services district, and any other information DOHMH may specify in its
rules.

Requires DOHMH to issue a new performance summary card at least once
every twelve months. The child care service must display this card
conspicuously at or near the entrance of its facility.

Section 2: Establishes an effective date.

 EXISTING LAW :

Under current law, child care services inside New York City are not
required to post their inspection reports at their facilities.
Outside of New York City, regulated child care providers are required
to do so under statutory requirements and regulations promulgated by
the Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS).

 JUSTIFICATION :

Parents deserve comprehensive, easily-understandable, and
readily-available information about the day care centers where they
plan to send their children. Currently, information detailing the
inspection histories of day cares is available online, but many
parents don't know how or where to access this information. Providing
this information in an easy to understand performance summary card
posted prominently at child care services' facilities will tell
parents that facilities are licensed and regulated, operating legally
under the laws of New York City; that a facility is registered
demonstrates that the facility is being inspected and is applying a
rigorous set of health and safety standards mandated by New York City.
The posting will also inform parents as to whether the facility is
consistently complying with the health and safety regulations placed
upon it via statute and regulation. Finally, it will help parents to
compare the record of the facility they're visiting against the
records of other facilities in the same social services district.

While OCFS may require day care centers to post their recent
inspection reports outside New York City, no such requirement exists
for day care centers regulated by New York City.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

This is a new bill.
 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None.

 LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None.

summary: Requires the department of health and mental hygiene in a city having a population of one million or more to issue a performance summary card to each child care service.
